cmdb: Configuration management database: the official record of every IT system and what depends on what. Change approvers use it to judge what a change will affect.
ci: Configuration item: one record in the CMDB, such as a server, a database, an application or an interface.
drift: A gap between what the CMDB records and what the evidence shows systems actually do, for example a connection that exists but was never recorded.
blast-radius: Everything that stops working, directly or further down the chain, if one component fails or is taken down for a change.
declared-observed: Declared: written in the CMDB by people. Observed: seen in the evidence from discovery tools. Where the two disagree, that is drift.
hl7: The message standard hospitals use to move clinical data, such as lab results and orders, between systems.
interface: A feed that carries HL7 messages from one system to another, for example critical lab results to an Emergency department.
service-offering: One concrete part of a business service for one place or group, such as the critical results feed of one hospital's Emergency department.
business-service: Something the hospital provides that people notice when it stops, such as Emergency care, Pharmacy or Lab reporting.
discovery-source: A tool that reports what systems actually do: network scanners, traffic metrics, the interface engine, backup software and access logs.
change-request: A planned piece of IT work, such as a patch or an upgrade, that must be reviewed and approved before it happens.
agent: A program that uses an AI model to decide its own next step: here it chooses graph queries one at a time, then gives a checked verdict and acts (notes, alerts, proposed fixes).
mcp: Model Context Protocol: an open standard for offering tools to AI models. The graph queries are an MCP server, so the agent (or any MCP client) can list and call them.
memory-graph: A separate FalkorDB graph where the agent stores its investigations and what people approved or rejected, so it can recall them next time.
fhir: Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources: the modern web standard (HL7 FHIR) for reading patient records through an API; SMART on FHIR apps use it.

drift_types.D1: Undocumented dependency: the evidence shows one system using another, but the CMDB has no such relationship.
drift_types.D2: Stale relationship: the CMDB lists a dependency that no evidence has seen in the observed period, and it is not a failover link.
drift_types.D4: Retired CI still linked: a system marked retired in the CMDB still has relationships.
drift_types.D5: Owner drift: the team recorded as owner is not the team that actually resolves its incidents and makes its changes.
drift_types.D6: Shadow IT: a system found on the network by discovery that is not in the CMDB at all.
drift_types.D7: Ghost CI: a CMDB record in a scanned network that no scan or traffic has ever seen.
drift_types.D8: Attribute drift: a recorded detail (operating system version, serial number or IP address) differs from what discovery reports.
drift_types.D9: Protection-path drift: patient data whose storage never reaches another site, although the CMDB says there is an off-site copy.
drift_types.D10: Backups failing: the CMDB says the system is backed up, but its last successful backup is more than a week old.
drift_types.D11: Data residency: patient data is copied to a location where it must not be stored.
drift_types.D12: Access drift: access that no grant explains, by a disabled account, or admin work outside an approved change window.
drift_types.D13: Naming mismatch: one system known by different names in different tools; matched by serial number or IP, not a real problem.
drift_types.D14: Unregistered app: a third-party app reads patient records through the EMR's FHIR API but is registered nowhere.

sources.cmdb_export: The hospital's own record, exported from its CMDB tool: what people have declared.
sources.discovery_scanner: A network scanner that walks the data centres and clinics and lists every device it can reach.
sources.apm_otel: Application monitoring that traces which applications call which databases and services.
sources.netflow: Traffic summaries from the network routers: who talks to whom, including medical devices with no software agent.
sources.interface_engine: The hub that routes HL7 messages between clinical systems; its configuration shows where messages really go.
sources.backup_software: The backup system's job history: what is really backed up, and whether a copy leaves the building.
sources.storage_telemetry: The storage arrays' own reports on which volumes are replicated to the other data centre.
sources.identity_sso: Single sign-on logs: which staff sign in to which applications, from which workstation.
sources.db_audit: Database audit logs: who reads, changes and administers the production databases.
sources.hr_feed: The HR system's list of staff and their employment status, to spot accounts of people who have left.
sources.itsm_history: The IT service desk's history: which team really fixes incidents and carries out changes on each system.
